# Part 2: Putting categories in order (factors)

R sorts text **alphabetically**:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 2.1** — `count()` the age groups. What order are they in?
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>% count(age_cat)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   age_cat    n
1    18-29 1455
2    30-39  582
3    40-49  245
4    50-59   77
5    60-69   27
6    70-79    6
7      80+    1
8 Under 18 3962
9  Unknown   96
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `count(age_cat)` lists the age groups in **alphabetical** order. Numbers sort before letters, so "18-29" comes first, and the biggest group, "Under 18" (3962 cases), ends up after "80+".
-   This order would carry into every table and plot, which is why you set a better one next.
:::

"Under 18" should come first, and "Unknown" last. A **factor** is a text column with a set order of categories (called **levels**). `fct_relevel()` from the forcats package (part of the tidyverse) sets that order:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 2.2** — Put `age_cat` and `outcome` in order with `fct_relevel()` (the next two code blocks).

Pattern: `DATA <- DATA %>% mutate(COLUMN = fct_relevel(COLUMN, "LEVEL_1", "LEVEL_2", ...))`
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist <- linelist %>%
  mutate(age_cat = fct_relevel(age_cat,
    "Under 18", "18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80+", "Unknown"
  ))

linelist %>% count(age_cat)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   age_cat    n
1 Under 18 3962
2    18-29 1455
3    30-39  582
4    40-49  245
5    50-59   77
6    60-69   27
7    70-79    6
8      80+    1
9  Unknown   96
```


:::
:::


The order carries through to every table **and** every plot. Other useful forcats functions:

-   `fct_infreq()` — order by how common each category is (most common first)
-   `fct_rev()` — reverse the order
-   `fct_relevel(x, "Unknown", after = Inf)` — move one category to the end


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist <- linelist %>%
  mutate(outcome = fct_relevel(outcome, "Recover", "Death", "Unknown"))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `fct_relevel(age_cat, "Under 18", "18-29", ...)` turns `age_cat` into a factor and sets its levels in the order you list them. `mutate()` puts the result back in the same column, and `linelist <-` saves it.
-   `count(age_cat)` now goes from youngest to oldest, with "Unknown" last. The counts didn't change, only the order.
-   The second block does the same for `outcome`: Recover, Death, Unknown.
-   Each level has to be spelled exactly as in the data, capitals included.
:::

::: callout-note
A `.csv` file can't store factor order at all. An `.rds` file can, but the files we saved in Session 3 contain plain text columns, so you set the order again after importing.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Misspelling a level: `fct_relevel()` warns "Unknown levels" and ignores it.
:::

::: callout-note
## 🔁 The base R way: `factor()`

In other people's code you will see `factor(x, levels = c(...))`. It sets the order too, but a misspelled level is **not** ignored with a warning: every value that doesn't match becomes `NA`, silently (reading only, you don't need to type this):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
factor(c("Recover", "Death", "Death"), levels = c("Recover", "Death"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] Recover Death   Death  
Levels: Recover Death
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
factor(c("Recover", "Death", "Death"), levels = c("Recover", "death"))   # oops: NA, no warning
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] Recover <NA>    <NA>   
Levels: Recover death
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   The first line makes a factor with the levels Recover, Death. R prints the values, then a `Levels:` line with their order.
-   In the second line, "death" (lower case) matches none of the values, so both "Death" values become `<NA>`, and R doesn't warn you. `fct_relevel()` would have.
:::

`levels(x)` shows the order of any factor. The forcats functions are safer for day-to-day work; `factor()` is what you need to read.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}

One `mutate()` can change several columns at once. The age groups now go from youngest to oldest, with "Unknown" last.
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📖 Good to know

-   A factor stores each value as a number that points to its list of levels: that's how it remembers the order. `levels(x)` shows the list, and `as.character(x)` turns a factor back into plain text.
-   The order matters in statistics too: in a regression model, the **first** level is the reference group that the others are compared with.
:::

# Part 3: Counting and percentages with `count()`

## Counts and cross-tabs

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.1** — `count(outcome)`, then `count(age_cat, outcome)`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>% count(outcome)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  outcome    n
1 Recover 2158
2   Death 2840
3 Unknown 1453
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Two columns: every combination
linelist %>% count(age_cat, outcome)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    age_cat outcome    n
1  Under 18 Recover 1322
2  Under 18   Death 1755
3  Under 18 Unknown  885
4     18-29 Recover  498
5     18-29   Death  648
6     18-29 Unknown  309
7     30-39 Recover  179
8     30-39   Death  256
9     30-39 Unknown  147
10    40-49 Recover   85
11    40-49   Death  105
12    40-49 Unknown   55
13    50-59 Recover   24
14    50-59   Death   29
15    50-59 Unknown   24
16    60-69 Recover   16
17    60-69   Death    8
18    60-69 Unknown    3
19    70-79 Recover    3
20    70-79   Death    3
21      80+ Recover    1
22  Unknown Recover   30
23  Unknown   Death   36
24  Unknown Unknown   30
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `count(outcome)` gives one row per outcome: Recover 2158, Death 2840, Unknown 1453. The rows follow the factor order you set in Part 2.
-   `count(age_cat, outcome)` counts every combination of age group and outcome that occurs: 24 rows. Combinations with no cases, such as 80+ and Death, are left out.
:::

## Percentages

`count()` makes a column called `n`. Divide by the total to get a proportion, and use `scales::percent()` to show it nicely:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.2** — Add a percent column to `count(outcome)`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(percent = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  outcome    n percent
1 Recover 2158   33.5%
2   Death 2840   44.0%
3 Unknown 1453   22.5%
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `count(outcome)` puts the counts in a column called `n`.
-   Inside `mutate()`, `sum(n)` is the total of that column (6451), so `n / sum(n)` is each outcome's share: 2840 / 6451 = 0.440 for Death.
-   `scales::percent(..., accuracy = 0.1)` shows 0.440 as "44.0%". `accuracy = 0.1` means one decimal place. The result is text: easy to read, but not for further calculations.
:::

## Percentages within groups: `group_by()`

`group_by()` makes the next steps happen **separately for each group**. Here, `sum(n)` becomes the total *within each age group*, so each age group adds up to 100%:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.3** — Percentages within each age group with `group_by()`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  group_by(age_cat) %>%
  count(outcome) %>%
  mutate(percent = scales::percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) %>%
  ungroup()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 24 × 4
   age_cat  outcome     n percent
   <fct>    <fct>   <int> <chr>  
 1 Under 18 Recover  1322 33.4%  
 2 Under 18 Death    1755 44.3%  
 3 Under 18 Unknown   885 22.3%  
 4 18-29    Recover   498 34.2%  
 5 18-29    Death     648 44.5%  
 6 18-29    Unknown   309 21.2%  
 7 30-39    Recover   179 30.8%  
 8 30-39    Death     256 44.0%  
 9 30-39    Unknown   147 25.3%  
10 40-49    Recover    85 34.7%  
# ℹ 14 more rows
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `group_by(age_cat)` splits the rows into one group per age group. The data looks the same, but the next steps run once for each group.
-   `count(outcome)` then counts the outcomes inside each age group.
-   In `mutate()`, `sum(n)` is now the total **of that age group**, so each age group adds up to 100%. For example, 44.3% of the under-18s died (1755 of 3962).
-   `ungroup()` removes the grouping, so later steps work on all the rows again.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: how is this different from `count(age_cat, outcome)` without `group_by()`?

Without grouping, the percentages are out of all 6,451 cases, so all the rows together add up to 100%. With `group_by(age_cat)`, each age group adds up to 100% on its own.
:::

::: callout-tip
## `ungroup()` when you're done

A grouped data frame stays grouped. End with `ungroup()` so later steps don't surprise you.
:::

::: callout-note
## 🔁 The base R way: `table()` and `prop.table()`

Base R makes a cross-table with `table()` (from Session 1), and turns it into proportions with `prop.table()`. `margin = 1` makes each **row** add up to 1, like `group_by(age_cat)` above (reading only, you don't need to type this):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
age_outcome <- table(linelist$age_cat, linelist$outcome)
age_outcome
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `table(linelist$age_cat, linelist$outcome)` makes a cross-table: age groups down the side, outcomes across the top, and a count in each cell. It's saved as `age_outcome` so you can reuse it.
-   `prop.table(age_outcome, margin = 1)` divides each cell by its row total, so each row adds up to 1. `* 100` and `round(..., 1)` turn that into percentages: the same numbers as the `group_by()` version (44.3 for Under 18 and Death).
-   Unlike `count()`, `table()` shows combinations with no cases as 0.
:::

The result is a `table`, not a data frame, so it doesn't work with `filter()`, `mutate()`, or ggplot. That is why we use `count()` in this workshop.
:::

# Part 4: Summary statistics with `summarise()`

`summarise()` collapses many rows into **one row** of results. You name each new column on the left of `=`.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 4.1** — `summarise()` the number of cases and the mean, SD, and median age for everyone.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    mean_age   = mean(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_age     = sd(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_age = median(age_years, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
     n mean_age   sd_age median_age
1 6451 16.05732 12.64829         13
```


:::
:::


`na.rm = TRUE` means "skip missing values". Without it, one `NA` makes the whole result `NA`.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `summarise()` collapses all 6451 rows into one row. Each `name = calculation` inside it makes one column of the result.
-   `n()` counts the rows: 6451.
-   `mean()` is the average age (about 16.1 years). `sd()` is the standard deviation (about 12.6): how spread out the ages are. `median()` is the middle value: 13.
-   96 patients have no age, so without `na.rm = TRUE` the mean, SD, and median would all be `NA`.
:::

## By group

Add `group_by()` first to get **one row per group**:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 4.2** — The same by outcome, plus the mean BMI and mean temperature.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  group_by(outcome) %>%
  summarise(
    n          = n(),
    mean_age   = mean(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_age = median(age_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_bmi   = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_temp  = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 6
  outcome     n mean_age median_age mean_bmi mean_temp
  <fct>   <int>    <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Recover  2158     16.1         13     30.6      38.6
2 Death    2840     15.9         13     30.7      38.6
3 Unknown  1453     16.2         14     30.4      38.6
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🧩 Reading a function call

Here is a shorter version of the code above, taken apart:

`linelist %>% group_by(outcome) %>% summarise(n = n(), mean_age = mean(age_years, na.rm = TRUE))`

| Piece | What it is | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `linelist` | the data | where the steps start |
| `%>%` | the pipe | passes the result on its left into the next function, as its first argument |
| `group_by(outcome)` | a dplyr function | splits the rows into one group per outcome |
| `summarise(...)` | a dplyr function | collapses each group into one row of results |
| `n = n()` | a new column called `n`, made by the function `n()` | counts the rows in each group |
| `mean_age = mean(age_years, ...)` | a new column called `mean_age`, made by `mean()` | the average age in each group |
| `na.rm = TRUE` | a named argument of `mean()` | "remove NAs": skip the missing ages |

Inside `summarise()`, the name on the **left** of `=` is the new column, and the calculation is on the **right**. With the pipe, R runs the steps from **left to right**. Read each `%>%` as "and then": "take `linelist`, and then group it by outcome, and then summarise: `n` is the number of rows, and `mean_age` is the mean of `age_years`, skipping missing values."
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `group_by(outcome)` before `summarise()` gives one row **per outcome** instead of one row for everyone.
-   Each row is calculated only from its own group: 2158 patients who recovered, 2840 who died, and 1453 with an unknown outcome.
-   In this fictional dataset the groups are very similar: the median age is 13 for both recovered and died, and the mean temperature is 38.6 °C in all three groups.
:::

::: callout-note

## 🔍 What this code does

-   `filter(outcome != "Unknown")` keeps the 4998 patients with a known outcome, and `fct_drop()` removes the now-empty "Unknown" level.
-   `select()` chooses what goes in the table: each selected column becomes one variable in Table 1. `by = outcome` makes the outcomes the column groups.
-   `tbl_summary()` works out each column's type. Categories (like `gender`) show count (%). Numbers (like `age_years`) show the median and, in brackets, the 25th and 75th percentiles: 13 (6, 23) years for patients who recovered.
-   The headers show the size of each group: N = 2,158 recovered and N = 2,840 died.
-   Two kinds of "Unknown" appear: our own "Unknown" text values, shown as a category (86 recovered patients have an unknown gender), and gtsummary's row for missing values, which it also calls "Unknown" (30 missing ages). The next step sorts this out.
:::

"Unknown" shows up as a category. In Session 3 we replaced `NA` with "Unknown" so missing values show up in counts — but `tbl_summary()` has its own **Missing** row, so turn "Unknown" back into `NA` for this table with `na_if()`:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 6.2** — The same table with `na_if()`, so "Unknown" counts as missing.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist %>%
  filter(outcome != "Unknown") %>%
  mutate(outcome = fct_drop(outcome)) %>%
  select(outcome, gender, age_years, age_cat, bmi, hospital_name, fever, cough, temp) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, "Unknown"))) %>%
  tbl_summary(by = outcome)
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, "Unknown")))` goes through every text column (`where(is.character)`) and replaces the value "Unknown" with `NA`.
-   Gender's unknowns (86 and 139) move from a category into the missing-values row.
-   `fever` and `cough` now only have "yes" and "no", so gtsummary shows them on one line: the number with "yes". For fever that's 1,708 (82%) of the patients who recovered. The percentage is now out of patients whose fever status is known, which is why it's higher than the 79.1% in Part 4.
-   `age_cat` is a factor, not text, so `where(is.character)` skips it and its "Unknown" stays a category.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   After `filter(outcome != "Unknown")`, the empty level is still there. `fct_drop(outcome)` removes it, or `tbl_summary()` shows an empty column.
:::

## Customize it

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 6.3** — A customized `table1` with labels, mean (SD), an overall column, bold labels, and a caption; then save it to `outputs/table1.docx` (the next two code blocks).
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
table1 <- linelist %>%
  filter(outcome != "Unknown") %>%
  mutate(outcome = fct_drop(outcome)) %>%
  select(outcome, gender, age_years, bmi, hospital_name, fever, cough, temp) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, "Unknown"))) %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = outcome,
    label = list(
      gender        ~ "Gender",
      age_years     ~ "Age (years)",
      bmi           ~ "BMI",
      hospital_name ~ "Hospital",
      fever         ~ "Fever",
      cough         ~ "Cough",
      temp          ~ "Temperature (°C)"
    ),
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
    missing_text = "Missing"
  ) %>%
  add_overall() %>%
  bold_labels() %>%
  modify_caption("**Table 1. Patient characteristics by outcome**")
```

## 🔍 What this code does

-   `label = list(gender ~ "Gender", ...)` gives each row a readable name. Read each `~` as "gets the label".
-   `statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})"` shows mean (SD) instead of median and percentiles for every number column. gtsummary fills in the words in `{ }`.
-   `missing_text = "Missing"` renames gtsummary's missing-values row from "Unknown" to "Missing", so it can't be confused with a category.
-   `add_overall()` adds a column for all patients together, `bold_labels()` makes the variable names bold, and `modify_caption()` adds the title (the `**` make it bold).
-   In the second block, `as_flex_table()` turns the table into a flextable, and `flextable::save_as_docx()` writes it to the Word file `outputs/table1.docx`.

## 📖 Good to know

-   A Table 1 usually shows categories as n (%) and numbers as median (IQR) or mean (SD), and reports missing values. Many journals, and the CONSORT guidelines for trials, advise against p-values in a Table 1 that describes the groups.
-   If something in the Word table needs to change, change the code and save the table again, rather than editing the Word file by hand. That way the table always matches the data.

# Key points

-   **Factors** set the order of categories; `fct_relevel()` puts them in a sensible order that carries through to every table and plot.
-   `count()` counts categories; `mutate(percent = n / sum(n))` adds percentages.
-   `group_by()` makes the next steps happen separately for each group — end with `ungroup()`.
-   `summarise()` collapses rows into summary statistics; use `na.rm = TRUE` to skip missing values, and `across()` to do the same thing on many columns.
-   `tabyl()` + the `adorn_*()` functions (in order: totals, percentages, formatting, ns, title) make quick cross-tabs.
-   `tbl_summary()` makes a publication-ready Table 1; `as_flex_table()` + `flextable::save_as_docx()` saves it to Word.
